title: Dion3: Making Muon's Orthogonalization Cheap
hook: Muon trains faster than AdamW but pays for it in a cubic-time orthogonalization step. Dion3 attacks that overhead at every layer of the stack — up to 6x faster optimizer steps at matching loss.
key_points: Muon's Newton–Schulz orthogonalization is cubic-time, and sharded weights add communication cost on top.
A Gram-based Newton–Schulz variant cuts the FLOPs; custom CuteDSL kernels exploit symmetry for more speed.
Megabatching reduces the communication overhead when the optimizer state is sharded across devices.
The update rule orthogonalizes only a fraction of the momentum matrix's rows each step.
Authors report matching or beating Muon's loss with up to 6x lower optimizer step time.
Shipped in Microsoft's `dion` package as a drop-in Muon replacement.
content_html: The Muon optimizer beats AdamW on wall-clock training, but its central trick — orthogonalizing each layer's momentum update via a Newton–Schulz iteration — is cubic-time, and when weights are sharded across GPUs the communication cost compounds it. In many real setups that overhead eats the win. Dion3 is a revision of Muon that attacks the cost at every level of the stack.
extra_html:
What changed

Three engineering layers plus one algorithmic one. A Gram Newton–Schulz algorithm reduces the FLOP cost of the orthogonalization itself. CuteDSL kernels accelerate it further by exploiting the symmetry of the matrices involved. A megabatching strategy cuts the communication overhead in the sharded case. On top of those, the authors change the update rule: rather than orthogonalizing the whole momentum matrix, select only a fraction of its rows each step. They report this improves on Dion — an earlier "compressed" Muon variant — in both speed and quality.

Why it matters

Optimizer overhead is the kind of thing that decides whether a research result becomes production practice. Muon's advantage is real but was partly theoretical once you accounted for the step cost at scale; the authors report Dion3 matches or improves Muon's loss with optimizer step time reduced by up to 6x. It ships in Microsoft's dion package as a drop-in replacement, which is what turns a paper into something people actually run.

related.title: Muon: An Optimizer for Hidden Layers
related.hook: Muon orthogonalizes each gradient update before applying it — and trained networks faster than AdamW, the first serious challenger to Adam's reign in years.

related.title: Why Muon Skips Gradient Descent's Slow Start
related.hook: Small-init gradient descent crawls through a 'saddle-to-saddle' bottleneck — Muon skips it, learning every mode at once and staying stable past where gradient descent blows up.

related.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations for Trillion-Parameter Models
related.hook: Data-parallel training wastes memory by copying optimizer states, gradients, and parameters onto every GPU. ZeRO partitions them instead — fitting 100B+ parameter models.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main cost Dion3 is trying to remove from Muon?
flashcards.back_html: The cubic-time Newton–Schulz orthogonalization step — plus the communication overhead that compounds it when weights are sharded across devices.

flashcards.prompt: Which change to the update rule does Dion3 make to cut cost further?

choices.text: Orthogonalize only a fraction of the momentum matrix's rows each step
Skip orthogonalization entirely on every other step
Replace the momentum matrix with its diagonal

flashcards.explanation_html: Dion3 selects a subset of the momentum matrix's rows to orthogonalize per step, which the authors report improves on Dion in both speed and performance.

flashcards.prompt: What does Dion3 claim about final model quality relative to Muon?

choices.text: It matches or improves Muon's loss while cutting step time up to 6x
It trades a small loss penalty for the speedup
It only matches Muon on small models

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper reports matching or improved loss versus Muon with optimizer step time reduced by up to 6x.
